p.n: The King Requests the Full Parable

body.p: “And how was that?” said the King. “The

p.n: The Rat and the Cat Live Next to a Tree

body.p:
claim goes,” said the Philosopher, “that
in such-and-such a place there was a great yabrūṭ tree at whose foot
was the burrow of a rat called Fayrūz and near that site was the dwelling of a
cat named Rūmī.

Huntsmen occasionally sought
game and fowl near that tree; and that one day one such huntsman set a snare of his
into which the cat fell.

“The rat came out creeping, to seek something to eat,
yet all the while cautious, turning around, surveying; upon seeing the cat trapped
in the snares, he rejoiced at it.

He then turned behind him and saw that a mongoose
had tracked him and lay in wait; and looking over his head, he saw an owl, atop the tree, watching him.
And so he feared-that if he turned back, the mongoose would jump on him; that if he moved
left or right, the owl would snatch him; and that if he stepped forward
the cat would eat him.

‘These are troubles that have besieged me,’ he said,
“and evils that have come upon me in succession, and I have no resort but to my sense and ingenuity. I should not be overtaken by confusion,
and my intelligence must not be scattered in dismay].

The sensible man does not lose judgment, and his intelligence
does not abandon him, whatever the circumstance;

for the minds of the intelligent are like the sea
whose depth cannot be reached.

p.n: Situations Do Not Blind the Intelligent

body.p:
